subject: Public health
summary: Human communication skills are essential for effective patient care, enabling clinicians to gather accurate histories, build trust, and convey complex information clearly. Mastery of these skills improves health outcomes, especially in low-resource settings.

sections.p: Human communication skills encompass verbal, non‑verbal, and written exchanges that facilitate understanding between clinician and patient. They are assessed through observation of interaction quality and patient feedback rather than a formal test.
Communication breakdowns are graded by impact: mild (misunderstanding), moderate (non‑adherence), severe (clinical harm). Staging guides intervention intensity.
Common causes include language barriers, cultural differences, low health literacy, clinician time pressure, and emotional distress.
Patients may ask irrelevant questions, repeat information, or show hesitation. Clinicians may appear rushed, use jargon, or ignore body language.
Assessment tools: Communication Assessment Tool, Patient Satisfaction Survey, and direct observation checklists.

t.b: High score indicates effective communication; low score flags need for improvement.
Low scores suggest barriers to understanding or trust.
Missing items point to training gaps.

sections.p: Red flags: repeated misunderstandings, patient refusal of care, or documented adverse events linked to miscommunication.
Interventions target both clinician and system: training in cultural competence, use of interpreters, simplified language, teach‑back method, and structured communication protocols.
Regular refresher courses, peer review of consultations, and patient feedback loops sustain skills. Prevention focuses on early identification of communication barriers.
Communication skills are distinct from medical knowledge; a well‑educated clinician may still lack effective communication.
Assuming patient understanding from verbal agreement can be misleading; objective checks like teach‑back are essential.

faq.q: Why is communication important in low-resource settings?
faq.a: It compensates for limited diagnostics by ensuring accurate history, adherence, and patient engagement.

faq.q: How can I improve my communication when time is short?
faq.a: Use concise, jargon‑free language, ask open questions, and confirm understanding with teach‑back.

faq.q: What if a patient speaks a different language?
faq.a: Employ trained interpreters, use visual aids, and avoid relying on family members for translation.

exam: Describe a strategy to ensure patient understanding in a multilingual clinic.
Explain how the teach‑back method reduces medication errors.
Identify three red flags that indicate a communication breakdown leading to adverse outcomes.
